extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers interested in 18th-century London fairs, popular entertainments, and theatre history
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length historical description of Bartholomew, Southwark, and other London fairs in the mid-18th century, focusing on showmen, booths, entertainments, advertising, and notable performers. Useful for understanding period practices, promotional conventions, and types of acts presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied medley entertainment (program variety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills advertise a medley entertainment comprising 'the surprising performances of M. Jano, M. Raynard, M. Baudouin, and Mynheer Vander Huff. Also a variety of rope-dancers, tumblers, posture-masters, balance-masters, and comic dancers' and concluding items such as 'Italian Shadows' and a 'grand ballet dance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers promoted a large variety of acts (comic dances, pantomimes, shadow-plays, rope-dancing, tumbling, music) in a single bill to attract broad audiences; variety was a central selling point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete band of music
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising promised 'With a complete band of music of hautboys, violins, trumpets, and kettle-drums.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full instrumental band was used as a marker of production quality; inclusion of named instruments signalled scale and legitimacy of the entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of decorations and scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: The bills assert 'All the decorations entirely new' and 'The scenes and clothes are entirely new.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit claims of new scenery and costumes were used to advertise freshness; novelty in visual presentation was emphasized to entice repeat visitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance schedule and long hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Notations like 'To begin every day at one o'clock, and continue till eleven at night' and other bills beginning 'each day at twelve o'clock.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows ran long hours daily during the fair; published start and end times were part of marketing and accessibility expectations for audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility, illumination, and carriage access
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements note 'The passage to the booth is commodiously illuminated by several large moons and lanthorns, for the conveniency of the company, and that persons of quality's coaches may drive up the yard.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illumination and coach access were explicitly advertised to reassure and attract wealthier patrons and signal convenience and respectability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor duties and multi-skilled performance expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: A listed account of an actor's duties: 'an actor must sleep in the pit, and wake early to throw fresh sawdust into the boxes; he must shake out the dresses, and wind up the motion-jacks; he must teach the dull ones how to act, rout up the idlers from the straw, and redeem those that happen to get into the watch-house... sometimes he should dance... sing... blow the trumpet... laugh and joke... give them a kind of a touch-and-go speech... go into the crowd... shout opposite his own booth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers were expected to be highly versatile (acting, singing, dancing, instrument-playing, stagecraft, crowd-promotion, maintenance). Successful booth actors combined backstage labour, multiple stage skills, and active self-promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of material to pantomime/booth requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'Harlequin Scapin... the popular embodiment of Molière's humour was adapted with success to pantomimic requirements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers commonly adapted well-known plays or literary sources to pantomime or droll formats suited to fair audiences; fidelity to original form was less important than suitability to the medium and audience taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical and patriotic content as attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances concluded with items such as a chorus in praise of the Duke of Cumberland or songs lauding recent victories (e.g., references to Culloden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of patriotic or topical material was used to curry favour with audiences and authorities; loyalty-themed pieces could be purposeful marketing or crowd-pleasing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachronism tolerated for comic/popular effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers frequently introduced 'comic Englishmen of one type or another' into dramas 'without regard to the scene or the period of the drama to be represented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical accuracy was often sacrificed for immediate comic effect; audiences were generally not critical of anachronism, so managers prioritized recognisable humour over period fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered pricing and admission charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission charges advertised with ranges (examples: 'from sixpence to half-a-crown', 'sixpence and to Working People, Servants, and Children at Threepence', 'threepence to a shilling').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booths and exhibitions used tiered pricing—different prices for gentry vs working people, scaled admission—to maximize attendance across social classes and signal exclusivity where desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exotic, sensational, or curiosity attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Displays and adverts for 'the strange and wonderful monstrous production of Nature, a sea-elephant head', 'a young Oronutu savage', a 'female dwarf... the Amazing CORSICAN FAIRY', camels, hyænas, panthers, 'man-tigers', mermaids, and other prodigies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensational natural curiosities and human 'curiosities' were central draws; provenance and sensational description (measurements, origins, languages spoken) were emphasized to increase perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige and royal endorsement as promotional claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include performers having 'had the Honour of being shown three Times before their Majesties' or acts 'who have had the honour of performing before the Prince of Wales.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of royal or aristocratic patronage were used to confer legitimacy and attract larger or higher-status audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical and technological marvels in exhibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits advertised 'The movements of this exhibition were effected by clock-work' and a 'travelling post-chaise from Switzerland, which, without horses, keeps its stage for upwards of fifty miles a day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanized displays and alleged technological wonders were marketed as curiosities; mechanical sophistication functioned as a selling point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety, exposed trickery, and the limits of marvel
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of feats (e.g., a Turk juggling what appeared to be oranges that were actually painted lead balls; Cadman's fatal fall due to 'a faulty cord') highlight both sensational claims and real hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposed trickery could diminish the perceived marvellousness of an act; accidents and equipment failure were real risks—both could affect reputation and audience trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional verbosity and spectacle-focused copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills use hyperbolic, descriptive copy ('the most astonishing Part of the Human Species', 'the richest and most beautiful in England', detailed biographical and physical particulars) to present exhibits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exuberant promotional language—detailed measurements, glowing appraisals, and narrative backstories—was standard practice to create intrigue and persuade attendance.
